cards.front: In the history of vitalism, what rule tests a claim that something "needs life"?
cards.back: Do that thing with the life taken out. The test counts only as far as you can show the life is really gone.
cards.why: "Really gone" means gone by evidence the opponents of the day accepted; it is a rule for testing a claim, not a law of chemistry.
cards.quote: A claim that something "needs life" is tested by doing that thing with the life taken out.

cards.front: What did vitalism claim about the molecules of living things?
cards.back: That only living things could make them; they were supposed to carry a vital force that ordinary matter lacked.
cards.quote: Into the early nineteenth century many chemists held that the molecules of living things needed living things to make them.

cards.front: In Berzelius's day, what made a substance "organic"?
cards.back: Being obtained from a living thing (sugar from cane, urea from urine, fat from tallow). The category was defined by source, not by formula.
cards.quote: The category was defined chiefly by where a substance came from, not by its formula.

cards.front: How is organic chemistry defined today?
cards.back: As the chemistry of carbon compounds whatever their source, though simple ones such as CO₂, carbonates and CS₂ are conventionally filed under inorganic.
cards.quote: Today organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon compounds whatever their source

cards.front: Berzelius analysed organic and inorganic matter with the same methods. What, then, held up the wall between the two kingdoms?
cards.back: Not any difference in method, but the conviction that only life could make organic matter.
cards.quote: Berzelius analysed both kinds with the same methods, but the wall between them rested on the conviction that only life could make them.

cards.front: In 1828 Wöhler tried to make ammonium cyanate from a cyanate salt and ammonia. What crystallized when he evaporated the solution?
cards.back: Urea, the molecule the body makes to get rid of nitrogen, with no kidney involved.
cards.quote: When he evaporated the solution, the crystals were not the salt but urea, the very molecule your body makes to get rid of nitrogen.

cards.front: Contrast how ammonium cyanate and urea are held together.
cards.back: Ammonium cyanate is a salt of two ions held by charge, NH₄⁺ and OCN⁻. Urea is one neutral molecule held by covalent bonds, H₂N–C(=O)–NH₂.
cards.quote: Ammonium cyanate is a salt, two ions held together by charge: NH₄⁺ (ammonium) and OCN⁻ (cyanate).

cards.front: Compounds with the same formula and different connections are {{c1::isomers}}.
cards.back: Urea and ammonium cyanate were one of the founding cases.
cards.quote: Compounds with the same formula and different connections are isomers.

cards.front: Count the atoms in urea, H₂N–C(=O)–NH₂, and in ammonium cyanate, NH₄⁺ OCN⁻. Give each molecular formula.
cards.back: Urea: 2 N + 4 H (two NH₂) + 1 C + 1 O. Ammonium cyanate: NH₄⁺ gives 1 N + 4 H; OCN⁻ gives 1 O + 1 C + 1 N. Both are CH₄N₂O, so they are isomers.
cards.quote: Both come to one carbon, four hydrogens, two nitrogens and one oxygen: CH₄N₂O.

cards.front: What general idea about molecules does the conversion of ammonium cyanate into urea carry?
cards.back: What a molecule is depends on how its atoms are connected, not just on which atoms it contains.
cards.quote: what a molecule is depends on how its atoms are connected, not just on which atoms it contains.

cards.front: Describe the two steps by which ammonium cyanate becomes urea.
cards.back: 1. NH₄⁺ hands a proton to cyanate, giving ammonia (NH₃) and cyanic acid (HNCO). 2. Ammonia's nitrogen lone pair attacks the carbon of cyanic acid and a proton shifts, giving urea.
cards.quote: The nitrogen of ammonia uses its lone pair to attack the carbon of cyanic acid, and a proton shifts.

cards.front: Heating Wöhler's solution helped form urea. Did heat drive an uphill reaction?
cards.back: No. Urea is the more stable form by a wide margin. Warming only sped up a change that was already downhill; heat let the connections rearrange.
cards.quote: Warming did not force the change; it sped up one already downhill

cards.front: A solution holds the equilibrium A⁺ + B⁻ ⇌ AB. Water is evaporated so the species crowd together. Which way does the equilibrium shift, and why?
cards.back: Toward AB. Crowding favors the side with fewer particles, and two ions become one molecule.
cards.why: Same reasoning as evaporation pushing ammonium cyanate further toward urea in Wöhler's flask.
cards.quote: crowding the ions together favors the side with fewer particles, and two ions become one molecule

cards.front: The conversion of ammonium cyanate to urea releases heat. A 0.1 M solution is heated to boiling. Predict what happens to the equilibrium constant and to the composition.
cards.back: K falls, about twenty- to thirtyfold by 100 °C, because the reaction is exothermic. The solution is still over 90% urea, because the conversion is so far downhill.
cards.quote: The conversion releases heat, so warming lowers the equilibrium constant, about twenty- to thirtyfold by 100 °C, yet a boiling 0.1 M solution is still over 90% urea.

cards.front: At room temperature, a 0.1 M solution of ammonium cyanate comes to roughly 98–99% urea at equilibrium. About how much ammonium cyanate remains?
cards.quote: at room temperature a 0.1 M solution comes to roughly 98–99% urea at equilibrium

cards.front: You are a chemist in 1828, and to you organic means "obtained from a living thing." On what ground could you refuse to count Wöhler's urea as a refutation of vitalism?
cards.back: Ask where the cyanate came from. It was made from potassium ferrocyanide, produced by heating blood, horn or hoof with potash and iron. So he had only turned one substance of animal origin into another.
cards.quote: In 1828, cyanides and cyanates were made from a salt (potassium ferrocyanide) produced by heating blood, horn or hoof with potash and iron.

cards.front: By the rule of taking the life out, where did Wöhler's urea synthesis remove life, and where was it still standing?
cards.back: Life was out of the making of one molecule, but still standing in the starting materials.
cards.quote: It took life out of the making of one molecule but left it standing in the starting materials.

cards.front: Why was Kolbe's 1845 acetic acid synthesis harder for vitalists to dismiss than Wöhler's urea?
cards.back: It started from carbon disulfide, made by heating charcoal with sulfur, so nothing in the chain still carried life.
cards.why: It made the provenance objection (where the starting materials came from) hard to sustain, though it did not end vitalism on its own.
cards.quote: He started from carbon disulfide, made by heating charcoal with sulfur to red heat

cards.front: In the last step of Kolbe's acetic acid synthesis, battery current turned trichloroacetic acid into acetic acid. Was this an oxidation or a reduction, and what did the current supply?
cards.back: A reduction. The current supplied the electrons that swapped the last three chlorines for hydrogens.
cards.quote: its current supplied the electrons that swapped the last three chlorines for hydrogens

cards.front: Charcoal is usually made from wood. Why did that not reopen the vitalists' loophole for Kolbe's synthesis, and what does it reveal about what "life really gone" means?
cards.back: Once charred to carbon, charcoal counted for chemists of the day as an element, mineral matter with only a distant tie to life. So "really gone" means gone by evidence the opponents of the day accepted.
cards.why: Rests on the opening rule: a test counts only as far as you can show the life is really gone.
cards.quote: Charcoal is usually made from wood, but once charred to carbon it counted, for chemists of the day, as an element

cards.front: The two-carbon acetyl group enters the citric acid cycle carried as {{c1::acetyl-CoA}}.
cards.back: The acetyl group is the hub of metabolism, carried as acetyl-CoA in every cell of yours that has mitochondria.
cards.quote: carried as acetyl-CoA into the citric acid cycle in every cell of yours that has mitochondria

cards.front: In a triglyceride, each fatty acid joins glycerol by an {{c1::ester}} bond, releasing one water.
cards.quote: Each fatty acid joins the glycerol by an ester bond and releases one water.

cards.front: What is the reaction called when water is added to a fat and the reaction runs back to glycerol and fatty acids?
cards.back: Hydrolysis.
cards.quote: Add water and the reaction runs back: that is hydrolysis.

cards.front: Glycerol + 3 fatty acids ⇌ triglyceride + 3 H₂O. How much water is released when 2 mol of triglyceride form, and how much is consumed when 2 mol are fully hydrolyzed?
cards.back: 3 H₂O per triglyceride: 2 × 3 = 6 mol released on forming, and 6 mol consumed on full hydrolysis.
cards.quote: glycerol + 3 fatty acids ⇌ fat (a triglyceride) + 3 H₂O

cards.front: What did Berthelot's reversible synthesis and hydrolysis of fats show about the chemistry of the body's molecules?
cards.back: It is the same reversible, equilibrium chemistry that governs reactions in the mineral world, with no special law for the body's molecules.
cards.quote: This is the same reversible, equilibrium chemistry that governs reactions in the mineral world, with no special law for the body's molecules.

cards.front: Berthelot remade fats by joining glycerol and fatty acids taken from natural fats. By the rule of taking the life out, where was life removed and where was it still standing?
cards.back: Life was out of the joining step but still in the parts, since the glycerol and fatty acids came from natural fats. A partial test.
cards.quote: Life was out of the joining step, but his glycerol and fatty acids came from natural fats, so life was still in the parts.

cards.front: Sterile grape juice kept free of yeast stayed inert, while juice that yeast could reach fermented. What does this show, and what conclusion goes further than the data?
cards.back: Fermentation depends on living yeast. It does not show that fermentation is inseparable from the intact living cell; that line was stronger than the data required.
cards.quote: But from that true result Pasteur drew a line stronger than his data required: that fermentation was inseparable from the intact living cell.

cards.front: Who named the cell-free ferments "enzymes" in 1877, and what does the word mean?
cards.back: Wilhelm Kühne; from the Greek for "in leaven".
cards.quote: in 1877 Wilhelm Kühne named them enzymes, from the Greek for "in leaven"

cards.front: Pepsin and the invertase of yeast already worked outside cells before 1896. Why did that not settle whether life's chemistry needed the cell?
cards.back: The open question was the sugar-to-alcohol fermentation Pasteur had tied to life. For decades no one could make it run without cells.
cards.quote: could sugar-to-alcohol fermentation, the one Pasteur had tied to life, be pulled out of the cell too?

cards.front: Yeast is ground with sand and pressed to a clear juice with almost no intact cells, then sugar is added. The sugar ferments, with carbon dioxide rising. What does this show?
cards.back: Fermentation can run without intact living cells: the chemistry of metabolism can be lifted out of the cell and studied one reaction at a time.
cards.quote: The sugar began to ferment on its own, carbon dioxide rising through a flask of dead yeast

cards.front: Fermenting yeast juice is given three tests: a sterile filter that holds back every yeast cell, saturation with chloroform (an antiseptic), and gentle warming. Which tests can tell surviving cells from a dissolved chemical, and why?
cards.back: The filter and chloroform: cells predict fermentation stops, a dissolved chemical predicts it continues, and it continued. Warming cannot decide, since heat kills cells and also destroys a fragile dissolved substance.
cards.why: A test decides only if the two hypotheses predict different results.
cards.quote: A test decides only if the two answers predict different results, so the filter and the antiseptic decide it

cards.front: A lab claims that a reaction in a tissue extract needs living cells, and supports it by showing that heating the extract stops the reaction. Is that evidence sound? Name a test that would decide.
cards.back: Not sound: heat stops both a living cell and a fragile dissolved catalyst, so both hypotheses predict the same result. Sterile filtration or an antiseptic decides, because cells predict a stop and a dissolved chemical predicts the reaction continues.
cards.why: Rests on the rule from yeast-juice fermentation: a test decides only if the two answers predict different results.
cards.quote: Warming fails because both predict the same result.

cards.front: What carried the fermenting activity of cell-free yeast juice, and what was it named?
cards.back: A dissolved substance that Buchner judged undoubtedly a protein; he named it zymase.
cards.quote: must be regarded to be a dissolved substance, undoubtedly a protein.

cards.front: Zymase, the fermenting agent of yeast juice, turned out not to be one substance. What was it?
cards.back: A team: enzymes plus small heat-stable cofactors, chief among them cozymase, now known as NAD. Together they are glycolysis plus the two steps that make ethanol.
cards.quote: Harden and Young later split it into enzymes plus small heat-stable cofactors, chief among them cozymase, now known as NAD.

cards.front: Zymase is a team of enzymes plus small heat-stable cofactors such as NAD. Gentle warming stops fermentation in cell-free yeast juice. Which component most likely failed, and why?
cards.back: The enzymes. The cofactors are heat-stable, so the heat-sensitive part would be the protein catalysts (an inference).
cards.why: Combines the heat-stable cofactors with the warming result, where heat destroys a fragile dissolved substance.
cards.quote: Zymase turned out to be not one substance but a team

cards.front: After cell-free fermentation, a vitalist could still say "the zymase was made by yeast." What experiment closes that hatch, and what caveat remains?
cards.back: Build an enzyme from amino acids with no cell involved in the assembly, and show it works (first done in 1969, for ribonuclease A). Caveat: the amino acids were of biological origin, as with Berthelot's parts.
cards.why: Applies the rule again: take life out of one more place, and check whether it is really gone.
cards.quote: Build an enzyme from amino acids, with no cell involved in the assembly, and show it works.

cards.front: What premise replaced the vital force and underlies all of biochemistry?
cards.back: A living cell obeys the same chemistry as everything else. Its reactions can be pulled out, measured and explained by the same rules of structure, equilibrium and energy.
cards.quote: a living cell obeys the same chemistry as everything else

cards.front: What kind of molecule are nearly all biological catalysts (enzymes)?
cards.back: Nearly all of them are proteins.
cards.quote: The catalysts Kühne named and Buchner freed are, nearly all of them, proteins.

cards.front: Where in the human body is urea made, and by what pathway?
cards.back: In the liver, by five enzymes working in a loop called the urea cycle.
cards.quote: is built in your liver right now by five enzymes working in a loop called the urea cycle

cards.front: Urea can be made in a flask from a salt, and it is made in the liver by the enzymes of the urea cycle. What does this pair of facts say about defining "organic" by source, and about the chemistry of cells?
cards.back: The molecule is the same whatever made it, so a source-based definition of organic fails. The liver's route is ordinary chemistry run by protein catalysts: a cell obeys the same chemistry as everything else.
cards.why: Combines isomer structure (a molecule is its connections), the source-based definition of organic, and the premise that a cell obeys ordinary chemistry.
cards.quote: Life is chemistry, and chemistry can be measured, mapped, and understood.

cards.front: In 1926 urease, the enzyme that breaks down urea, was crystallized. What did this show, and why was it doubted at first?
cards.back: A catalyst of life could be held as a pile of crystals, argued to be a protein. Others doubted the crystals were the enzyme until more enzymes were crystallized in the early 1930s.
cards.quote: In 1926 James Sumner crystallized urease, the enzyme that takes urea back apart
